walkthroughs.body_html:
Density & Pressure — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Density & Pressure brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Density & Pressure.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A 200 g block has volume 100 cm³. Its density is:
options: 0.5 g/cm³
2 g/cm³
20 g/cm³
200 g/cm³

mcqs.q: An object will float in water if:
options: it is light
its mass is less than water's mass
its density is less than water's
it is hollow

mcqs.q: What does specific latent heat measure?
options: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 degree.
The temperature at which a substance melts or boils.
Gamma rays are slower than X-rays.
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.

mcqs.q: Why does a metal surface feel colder than a wooden surface in the same room?
options: The metal absorbs the heat from the air, leaving it colder than wood.
Gamma rays are slower than X-rays.
Metal conducts heat away from your hand more quickly than wood, so it removes thermal energy faster — even though both are at room temperature.
The metal is actually colder than the wood.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes gamma rays from X-rays of the same frequency?
options: Origin — gamma rays come from nuclear processes; X-rays come from electron transitions or deceleration of charged particles.
The metal absorbs the heat from the air, leaving it colder than wood.
Gamma rays have higher frequency than any X-ray.
Gamma rays are slower than X-rays.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Density”?
options: Mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V. Measured in kg/m³.
Force per unit area: P = F/A. Measured in pascals (Pa).
Pressure from the weight of air above a point; ~100 kPa at sea level, decreasing with altitude.
Upward force on an object in a fluid equal to the weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes' principle).
